10cbb4f4ee.q: How has AI inference spending changed for engineering teams at a16z crypto in the past three months?
10cbb4f4ee.a: In the past three months, a16z crypto's engineering team noticed that their ability to get more work done has become linear with the amount of money allocated to token budgets. Token spend has grown from a few thousand dollars monthly to a few hundred thousand dollars monthly, fundamentally changing how the team thinks about resource allocation from a capacity constraint to a budget allocation problem.
10cbb4f4ee.e: How AI is Changing the Way We Build Companies (ft. Guy Wuollet and Noah Citron)

c3bc071ace.q: What is the difference between treating token spend as headcount versus treating it as variable operational cost?
c3bc071ace.a: When token spend is treated like headcount, engineering organizations have a fuzzy sense of return on token and must make qualitative assessments. When treated as variable operational cost in specific business units, it can be scaled up or down rapidly, enabling more precise measurement of return on investment through mechanisms like A-B testing where token budgets are allocated to test specific hypotheses.
c3bc071ace.e: How AI is Changing the Way We Build Companies (ft. Guy Wuollet and Noah Citron)

1ddf7cfeb7.q: How can engineering teams use AI to autonomously run A-B tests and measure their impact on product metrics?
1ddf7cfeb7.a: Engineering teams can allocate a token budget for A-B tests and build autonomous agent systems that continuously generate hypotheses about which features to test, implement, and deploy potentially without human intervention. These systems can then measure how retention, churn, and other metrics change, while also tracking the actual cost of implementing each feature.
1ddf7cfeb7.e: How AI is Changing the Way We Build Companies (ft. Guy Wuollet and Noah Citron)

c0e52cb1d9.q: What makes the pod shop model difficult to apply to typical software engineering organizations?
c0e52cb1d9.a: In a pod shop, each portfolio manager has a clear individual P&L from their trading strategy. In software engineering, when multiple pods work on different parts of the same product with centralized revenue, it becomes very hard to measure each pod's individual contribution to overall P&L. This measurement difficulty makes the resource allocation problem much harder than in finance-based pod shops.
c0e52cb1d9.e: How AI is Changing the Way We Build Companies (ft. Guy Wuollet and Noah Citron)

ee0c813751.q: What financing model could better suit software businesses that need variable token spending rather than permanent headcount?
ee0c813751.a: Convertible debt, modernized private equity structures, or small-scale loans and investments could finance businesses that need significant token spending for a limited period to build a product, then operate as repeatable revenue engines. This model differs from venture capital, which expects permanent scaling, and maps to programmatic lending that underwriters can offer based on deterministic return-on-token metrics.
ee0c813751.e: How AI is Changing the Way We Build Companies (ft. Guy Wuollet and Noah Citron)

8ac2ab3377.q: What was the mental poker problem that inspired the invention of zero-knowledge proofs?
8ac2ab3377.a: The mental poker problem asked how two people sitting in different parts of the world could play cards over the phone without having any physical cards. They needed to deal a deck and play according to the rules while proving they followed those rules without revealing the cards or their encryption. This led Goldwasser and Micali to ask how to prove you're dealing cards properly without revealing everything about what you've encrypted and the randomness used to encrypt.
8ac2ab3377.e: How Zero-Knowledge Proofs Were Invented (ft. Co-Inventor and Turing Award Winner Shafi Goldwasser)

3f6c38f655.q: Why did interaction and randomness become essential to zero-knowledge proof design?
3f6c38f655.a: Interaction and randomness were introduced as the way to obtain privacy in cryptographic proofs. The verifier needed to accept a small chance of error, which enabled not revealing everything. This required modifying the notion of proof itself to allow for interactive protocols between a prover and verifier, rather than traditional non-interactive proofs. The definition of zero knowledge formalized that you will believe what is claimed but discover nothing else.
3f6c38f655.e: How Zero-Knowledge Proofs Were Invented (ft. Co-Inventor and Turing Award Winner Shafi Goldwasser)

b13f1b7ae6.q: What is the simulation paradigm in zero-knowledge proof verification?
b13f1b7ae6.a: The simulation paradigm is the way to formally define that a verifier learns nothing beyond the claim. It requires showing that whatever knowledge the verifier has after the interactive proof, they could have simulated that knowledge even without the prover and interaction occurring. Everything the verifier could do computationally before engaging in the proof interaction, they could do afterwards.
b13f1b7ae6.e: How Zero-Knowledge Proofs Were Invented (ft. Co-Inventor and Turing Award Winner Shafi Goldwasser)

3dfb694531.q: How did the GMR paper on zero-knowledge interactive proofs face rejection before publication?
3dfb694531.a: The paper on zero-knowledge proofs by Goldwasser, Micali, and Rackoff was submitted six times and kept getting rejected before finally being published. Despite the rejections, the authors remained determined, believing they had the right definition and that the work was very interesting. Goldwasser credits her co-author Silvio Micali's competitive nature as helping them persevere through the rejection process.
3dfb694531.e: How Zero-Knowledge Proofs Were Invented (ft. Co-Inventor and Turing Award Winner Shafi Goldwasser)

2f2e8afd29.q: What is the relationship between probabilistically checkable proofs and SNARKs in modern cryptography?
2f2e8afd29.a: Probabilistically checkable proofs use error-correcting codes to rewrite standard proofs so that if there was an error in the original classical proof, there would be many errors in the new one. This allows checking a proof by probing just a random location to detect errors. SNARKs compress these long proofs using Merkle trees and hash functions so they can be sent and verified while still allowing the verifier to poke at them and discover errors with high probability.
2f2e8afd29.e: How Zero-Knowledge Proofs Were Invented (ft. Co-Inventor and Turing Award Winner Shafi Goldwasser)

5e1952691e.q: Why is the SumCheck protocol particularly efficient for building modern SNARKs?
5e1952691e.a: The SumCheck protocol uses interaction extensively to force the prover to do work while keeping the verifier efficient and the proof short. It minimizes expensive cryptographic operations like hashing and group operations by using interaction strategically per variable rather than committing to large amounts of data upfront. This allows the protocol to avoid the overhead of committing to unnecessary data that would take longer to process and require additional proofs of validity.
5e1952691e.e: How Zero-Knowledge Proofs Were Invented (ft. Co-Inventor and Turing Award Winner Shafi Goldwasser)

b30676fc37.q: What safeguards does the Clarity Act include against money laundering and sanctions evasion?
b30676fc37.a: The Clarity Act has strict definitions of who is subject to anti-money laundering and sanctions requirements, applying all the same money laundering and treasury rules to crypto intermediaries that are applied in other markets. Financial intermediaries like Coinbase holding customer funds are subject to the same regulatory rules as fintechs like Stripe or PayPal, with clear definitions and black-and-white enforcement in the bill.
b30676fc37.e: Marc Andreessen and Chris Dixon: Why America Needs CLARITY

fb8a0de731.q: How would the Clarity Act have prevented the FTX collapse?
fb8a0de731.a: The Clarity Act provides federal regulatory oversight through the SEC and CFTC, requiring crypto exchanges to be federally registered with disclosure regimes, anti-fraud rules, and insider trading protections. FTX would have been required to be audited, maintain customer fund controls, and operate under surveillance regimes. Without compliance with these requirements, an exchange could not operate in the US, which would have prevented FTX's unauthorized movement of funds between entities.
fb8a0de731.e: Marc Andreessen and Chris Dixon: Why America Needs CLARITY

b5525af8e2.q: Why is regulatory clarity needed now for cryptocurrency when the industry developed without rules?
b5525af8e2.a: Stablecoin volumes now rival the size of the Visa network with trillions of dollars transacted quarterly, and major institutions like BlackRock, JP Morgan, Visa, and Fidelity have rushed into the market. Without a permanent regulatory framework similar to what exists for stocks and bonds, the industry remains vulnerable to catastrophes like FTX and lacks the consumer protections and institutional confidence needed for sustainable growth.
b5525af8e2.e: Marc Andreessen and Chris Dixon: Why America Needs CLARITY

5855ff8ae5.q: What is the difference between the Genius Act and the Clarity Act in regulating crypto?
5855ff8ae5.a: The Genius Act, which passed Congress and was signed by the president last year, provides a comprehensive regulatory framework specifically for stablecoins, which represent roughly 15% of the crypto market by market cap. The Clarity Act addresses the remaining 85% of the market, including blockchains themselves and other digital assets, providing federal regulatory frameworks for those areas that currently lack comprehensive guidance.
5855ff8ae5.e: Marc Andreessen and Chris Dixon: Why America Needs CLARITY

362e4127ed.q: How have stablecoin transaction costs changed since the early days of cryptocurrency?
362e4127ed.a: Three years ago, a stablecoin transaction might cost a couple of dollars or even tens of dollars, but now on most popular blockchains like Solana and Ethereum, transactions settle in sub-one-second timeframes and cost less than one penny, representing significant performance improvements equivalent to Moore's Law on blockchains.
362e4127ed.e: Marc Andreessen and Chris Dixon: Why America Needs CLARITY

9c8f535bc2.q: What motivated a leading complexity theorist to pivot toward algorithmic game theory and economic computation in the mid-1990s?
9c8f535bc2.a: Noam Nisan was inspired by the emergence of the Internet around 1995, which he saw as a massive paradigm shift that academia was too slow to embrace. He made a conscious decision to shift from computational complexity theory toward understanding how to get different computers to cooperate over the Internet, even when they do not belong to the same company or have the same goal. He initially tried to build systems but discovered that the most fascinating aspect was the economic and coordination problems of distributed cooperation.
9c8f535bc2.e: The 'Useless' Theory Behind Modern SNARKs (ft. Gödel Prize Winner Noam Nisan)

f35291a28f.q: How did the Popcorn project relate to ideas about verifying delegated computation?
f35291a28f.a: In the Popcorn project, Nisan and his team realized that if you delegate work to someone, you need a way to check it. They explored various checking methods: giving the work to multiple people to see if they get the same result, or using NP-like proofs. While they were thinking about distributed systems with issues of trust and incentives, they were not thinking about blockchain systems, but rather about how workstations on the web could cooperate and share resources even when not belonging to the same company or university.
f35291a28f.e: The 'Useless' Theory Behind Modern SNARKs (ft. Gödel Prize Winner Noam Nisan)

52d1ccab50.q: What is an interactive proof and why did it represent a fundamental extension of mathematical proof?
52d1ccab50.a: An interactive proof is a proof that uses both interaction and randomness, unlike traditional mathematical proofs. The key insight from work by Shamir, Goldreich, and Rakoff between 1984 and 1989 was that you need both interaction and randomness—if you only have one ingredient, you do not get anything new. This was mind-blowing for the community because interactive proofs could prove things in ways that are fundamentally different from conventional mathematical proofs.
52d1ccab50.e: The 'Useless' Theory Behind Modern SNARKs (ft. Gödel Prize Winner Noam Nisan)

3f4d3f65b6.q: How does the SumCheck protocol enable verification of computation across massive datasets and cloud computing?
3f4d3f65b6.a: Justin Thaler encountered the SumCheck protocol in a complexity theory course and later discovered it was instrumental for verifying cloud computation. The SumCheck protocol, from the LFKN paper, provides an efficient interactive proof mechanism that can be applied to streaming algorithms and massive datasets. Thaler found that for algorithms people care about with massive data sets, the SumCheck protocol serves as a universal solution—use SumCheck and you get optimal protocols for proving an untrusted prover solved the problem correctly, making it foundational to modern SNARKs.
3f4d3f65b6.e: The 'Useless' Theory Behind Modern SNARKs (ft. Gödel Prize Winner Noam Nisan)

2c99222eeb.q: What role did the LFKN paper play in establishing interactive proof systems for modern verification?
2c99222eeb.a: The LFKN paper from 1990-1992 established an efficient interactive proof for SharpSAT using the SumCheck protocol and demonstrated remarkable foresight. As Nisan notes, the paper had exactly the right protocol that researchers are still using today for modern SNARKs. The protocol emerged fully formed and elegant, and it became the centerpiece of complexity theory textbooks, showing that combining two concepts into one unified problem in computer science yields powerful results.
2c99222eeb.e: The 'Useless' Theory Behind Modern SNARKs (ft. Gödel Prize Winner Noam Nisan)

bdb18df698.q: How do modern SNARKs relate to interactive proofs and why is the SumCheck protocol central to current SNARK design?
bdb18df698.a: Modern SNARKs combine interactive proofs with commitment schemes. Justin Thaler explains that the GKR protocol from 2008 uses the SumCheck protocol as a subroutine, and these interactive proofs are essentially half of a SNARK. By combining them with cryptographic commitments, the result is the SNARKs with the fastest provers today. Thaler predicts that SNARKs using the SumCheck protocol at the core will eventually transform how digital infrastructure handles trust, as the prover speed is the key bottleneck keeping SNARKs from widespread adoption.
bdb18df698.e: The 'Useless' Theory Behind Modern SNARKs (ft. Gödel Prize Winner Noam Nisan)

3e685684b4.q: What unexpected connection emerged between random self-reducibility and interactive proofs for hard computational problems?
3e685684b4.a: Nisan discovered that Richard Lipton's proof of random self-reducibility for the permanent function could lead to an interactive proof. Initially Nisan could not believe Lipton's result because he knew that random self-reducibility could imply an interactive proof, yet the permanent is a notoriously difficult function. Upon closer inspection, he realized Lipton's approach worked because Lipton handled multiple instances rather than just one, enabling an interactive proof for this extremely hard problem.
3e685684b4.e: The 'Useless' Theory Behind Modern SNARKs (ft. Gödel Prize Winner Noam Nisan)
